svg.title: Site of origin: the BGP community that stops a dual-homed site learning its own prefix back
svg.desc: A topology with site 1 dual-homed to PE1 and PE2 through EIGRP, a backdoor path through the customer network, and the MPLS VPN in between. Four steps mark the mechanism. When PE1 redistributes EIGRP into MP-BGP it attaches a site-of-origin extended community with the value of site 1. The route travels through the VPN. When PE2 redistributes MP-BGP back into EIGRP, it compares the route's SoO with the local site identifier and refuses to install it because they match. The result is that the site never learns its own prefix back through the provider. A note contrasts this with a route tag, which only survives inside one protocol. A lower panel explains cost community as the companion mechanism that preserves the original EIGRP metric so the redistribution does not distort path selection.
svg.text: Site of origin answers one question: did this route come from here?
It is the only loop-prevention tool that survives the translation between two protocols
the customer's own backdoor between the two halves of site 1
It compares SoO with its own
Why not use a route tag?
A tag exists inside one protocol. Redistribution into BGP and back out again
does not carry it unless you map it by hand at every boundary.
SoO rides the BGP update itself, so every PE sees it for free.
Redistribution resets the EIGRP metric unless the original is carried along.
Cost community preserves it as an attribute, so the receiving site still ranks
paths by the customer's own notion of cost rather than by a seed value.
Design note: SoO is set per site, not per VRF. Two halves of one site share the same identifier on purpose — that is what makes the backdoor
safe. If two different sites are given the same value, they will refuse to learn each other's routes, and the symptom is a silent missing prefix.
